- The Hispanic unemployment rate fell from 12.8% in Q1 2010 to 6.4% in Q4 2015 and 5.6% in Q1 2016. (Page 6)
- The Hispanic unemployment rate remains above its low of 5% in Q4 2006 and is higher than the non-Hispanic rate in Q4 2015. (Page 6)
- Median household income for Hispanics was $42,491 in 2014, unchanged since the Great Recession. (Page 6)
- The Hispanic poverty rate was 23.6% in 2014, below the 2010 peak of 26.5% but above pre-recession levels. (Page 6)
- Hispanic households had the largest percentage decline in net worth through 2009, and their net worth continued to fall after the recession. (Page 6)
- A December 2015 Pew Research Center survey found 35% of Hispanics said economic conditions today are good or excellent, higher than the 25% of whites. (Page 7)
- 34% of Hispanics said U.S. economic conditions will be better in the coming year, about twice the share of other groups. (Page 7)

- 59% of Hispanics ages 65 and older expected their family finances to improve, which is the lowest share among major Hispanic demographic subgroups. (Page 8)
- 45% of Hispanics who rated their personal finances as "excellent" in 2015 expected their family's finances to improve "a lot." (Page 8)

- 59% of Hispanics describe their financial condition as "only fair" (47%) or "poor" (12%). (Page 9)
- In November 2008, only 4% of Latinos reported being in excellent financial shape and 19% said their condition was good. (Page 9)
- 30% of Latinos rated their financial condition as poor in 2008, more than double the share in 2015. (Page 9)

- 40% of Hispanics say their personal financial situation is in "excellent" (8%) or "good" (33%) shape (Page 9)
- 59% of Hispanics describe their financial condition as "only fair" (47%) or "poor" (12%) (Page 9)
- In November 2008, only 4% of Latinos reported being in excellent financial shape and 19% said their condition was good (Page 9)

- The share of Hispanics with a positive view of their finances has caught up to the general public: 43% of the general public versus 40% of Hispanics (Page 9)
- The gap between Latinos and the public regarding personal finances closed from 18 percentage points in 2008 to 3 percentage points in 2015 (Page 10)
- In 2008, 23% of Latinos rated their financial condition as excellent or good, compared to 40% in 2015, a +17 point change (Page 10)
- In 2004, 31% of Latinos had a positive view of their finances, which is lower than the current 40% (Page 10)
- The public's positive view of its finances was 51% in 2004 but is now lower (Page 10)
- Younger Hispanic adults (18-29) saw the largest gains, with 48% reporting an excellent or good financial shape in 2015, up from 21% in 2008 (+27 points) (Page 10)
- Gains in perceptions of economic well-being among Latinos 65 or older were modest at 37% in 2015 (Page 11)

- Positive views of economic well-being increased by 16 points among Latino men and 18 points among Latina women (Page 11)

- All of the increase in Hispanic optimism has occurred since 2011, when the share was 67%, growing to 73% in 2012 and 81% in 2015 (Page 13)

About seven-in-ten (72%) Hispanic adults expect their children will be better off financially than they themselves are, while 16% expect their children's financial situation will be about the same as theirs.
